text: [[amber|Amber]] is tree resin that hardened into stone over millions of years. Resin is the thick, sticky liquid that oozes from a cut in some trees, such as pines. It seals wounds and traps insects that might attack the tree.

When a small creature got stuck in the resin, more resin often flowed over it and sealed it in. Buried in soil and squeezed over time, the resin slowly hardened. The animal inside was kept in its exact shape, down to tiny hairs and the hooks on its legs. Amber gives us a window into ancient forests that ordinary [[fossil|fossils]] cannot.

No. DNA breaks down far too fast. Even in amber, none survives from the dinosaur age.

sec.t:
Most fossils form when bones or shells are buried in mud and turn to stone, as explained in [[@fossils-form|how a bone turns into stone]]. Amber works differently. The creature is not replaced by minerals. Its outline is sealed in a clear, golden case.

That is why amber fossils can show things that almost never survive, like the wings of gnats, spider webs and even a spider attacking its prey. Small animals are trapped most often: flies, beetles, [[@ants-farm|ants]] and mites. Bigger animals usually managed to pull free. Lizards, frogs and small feathers have been found, but they are rare.

In 2015, a scientist named Lida Xing was looking at amber in a market in Myanmar. One piece, being sold for jewellery, held something odd: a small, feathered tail. Tests showed it came from a young dinosaur, about 99 million years old.

The tail had bones as well as feathers, so it could not be a bird's tail feather. The [[@feathers|feathers]] were soft and fluffy, without the stiff central shaft of a flight feather. It was the first time anyone had seen dinosaur feathers in three dimensions, still attached to the body.

Amber from Myanmar raises hard questions, though. Some mines lie in conflict zones, and money from amber may fund fighting. In 2020, an international society of fossil scientists asked researchers to stop working on Myanmar amber bought after 2017.

{{story:static-electricity}}

India has its own famous amber. In a lignite coal mine near Vastan, in Gujarat's Surat district, scientists found lumps of amber about 52 million years old. Inside were hundreds of kinds of [[@lost-giant-insects|ancient insects]] and spiders.

This amber formed soon after India, which had been drifting north as an island, collided with Asia. Surprisingly, the creatures inside are close relatives of ones from other parts of the world. So animals may have crossed between India and Asia, or spread before India set off on [[@india-drift|its long journey]]. The resin came from trees in the same family as today's sal trees, still common in [[@forests-india|Indian forests]].

In the [[@hollywood|film]] Jurassic Park, scientists take dinosaur blood from a mosquito trapped in amber and use its [[@dna|DNA]] to bring dinosaurs back. It is a clever idea, but it would not work.

[[dna|DNA]] is a long, fragile [[molecule|molecule]]. After an animal dies, it starts to break into pieces. Studies of very old bones suggest that even in perfect conditions it is gone within a few million years at the most. The dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago. Amber seals the shape of a creature, but not its DNA.

Amber is light, only a little heavier than seawater, so storms in the Baltic Sea in northern Europe wash lumps of it onto the beaches. People there have collected Baltic amber for thousands of years to carve into beads and jewellery. Today amber is still sold as a gem, and every now and then a jeweller spots something with legs inside.

text: T. rex's arms were only about 1 metre long, on a body about 12 metres long. That is roughly the length of a grown-up's arm, on an animal as long as a city bus.

Its giant head and jaws did the hunting. Over millions of years, as tyrannosaur heads got bigger, their arms got smaller. Nobody knows for certain what the arms were still used for. In science, it's fine to say "we don't know yet". That's where new discoveries start.

Nobody knows for sure
To stay out of the way

st.reveal: It's a real mystery! The arms were strong. They might have lifted around 200 kg each. Ideas include gripping struggling prey, helping to get up, or shrinking so they didn't get bitten when several T. rex fed together. Scientists are still arguing.
st.nudge: That's one of the real ideas scientists have! But nobody has proven it yet.

sec.t:
The arms were stubby, but they were not weak. The bones were thick, and they show big rough patches where powerful [[@muscles|muscles]] were attached. In 2001, Kenneth Carpenter and Matt Smith studied some of the best-preserved T. rex arm bones. They estimated that the main arm muscle could have curled about 200 kg. That is more than two adults.

Each hand had two working fingers with sharp claws, plus a tiny third bone that did nothing much. The arm could swing only a short way at the shoulder and elbow. It couldn't reach the mouth.

For years, nobody even knew what the hands looked like. The first skeletons were found without them, so early drawings guessed, and some gave T. rex three fingers. A nearly complete arm was not found until 1988, in Montana, by a rancher named Kathy Wankel.

Muscles rarely fossilise, but they leave clues. Where a muscle grips a bone, it leaves a scar or a ridge. Bigger muscles leave bigger marks. Scientists compare these with living animals, mostly birds and [[@croc-ancient|crocodiles]], to work out the size and pull of muscles that vanished long ago. This is one of the tools in [[@how-reconstruct|rebuilding a dinosaur]] from its bones.

{{story:how-reconstruct}}

Scientists have suggested several uses.

One idea is that the arms held on to struggling prey, pinning it close to the chest while the jaws did the work. Another is that they helped T. rex push itself up from lying down, giving a little lift before the legs took over. A third is that they were used for gripping a partner during mating.

In 2022, Kevin Padian suggested something different. Maybe several T. rex sometimes fed on one [[carcass|carcass]] together. Long arms would have been in the way of all those snapping jaws, and easily bitten. Shorter arms could have been safer. Not everyone agrees, because we don't know for sure that T. rex fed in groups.

T. rex wasn't alone. The abelisaurs, a separate family of big hunters that included India's [[@rajasaurus|Rajasaurus]], ended up with even shorter arms. They weren't close relatives. Two different families arrived at a similar shape, probably because both relied on huge heads for hunting.

When the same feature [[evolve|evolves]] separately in different groups, scientists call it convergent [[evolution|evolution]]. Wings in bats and birds are another example. So are the streamlined bodies of dolphins and sharks, one a mammal and the other a fish.

Some body parts shrink because they are no longer much use. [[@whales-walked|Whales]] still carry tiny hip bones from their walking ancestors. Were T. rex's arms like that, slowly fading away? Their strong muscles suggest they still did something worth keeping. The answer may also be a mix: shrinking over time, yet still handy for a job or two.

myth: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain on Earth, from base to tip.

Everest has the highest summit above sea level. Measured from its base on the sea floor, Mauna Kea in Hawaii is taller, at over 10,000 m. And because Earth bulges at the equator, the top of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point farthest from Earth's centre.

sec.t:
Between India and Asia once lay an ocean called the Tethys. As [[@india-drift|India drifted north]], the floor of that ocean slid down beneath Asia. When India itself arrived, about 50 million years ago, its thick continental rock was too light to sink. The sea-floor rocks caught between were squeezed, folded and stacked up like a crumpled carpet.

The top of Everest is made of grey limestone that formed on the floor of the Tethys. It contains fossils of tiny sea creatures, such as [[@trilobites|trilobites]] and sea lilies. In the [[@spiti|Spiti valley]] of [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]], villagers find coiled ammonite fossils in the fields, more than 4,000 m above the sea.

At around 50 million years old, the Himalayas are [[@mountains-types|young for mountains]]. That's why they're so tall and sharp. Older mountains, like the Aravallis in Rajasthan, have been worn down for far longer. The [[@appalachians|Appalachian Mountains]] in the eastern USA are hundreds of millions of years old, and their rounded tops show it.

The Himalayas are still rising, by a few millimetres a year in places. But rain, rivers, ice and [[@landslides|landslides]] are wearing them down at the same time. The height of the peaks is a tug of war between the two.

India pushes into Asia by about 4 to 5 cm a year. That push builds up stress in the rocks, which is released in [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]]. In April 2015, a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck Nepal, causing great damage in Kathmandu and the villages around it, and setting off avalanches on Everest.

Scientists think some parts of the range have not had a big earthquake in centuries, so stress is still building there. That's why strong buildings matter so much in Himalayan towns.

Snow and [[@glaciers|glaciers]] in the Himalayas feed rivers like the Ganga, Indus and [[@brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]]. [[@rivers-himalaya|Follow a drop of the Ganga]].

The mountains hold so much ice that the region is sometimes called the Third Pole, after the Arctic and Antarctic. More than a billion people live along rivers that start in these mountains. The range also acts as a wall. It blocks freezing winds from Central Asia in winter, and it forces the monsoon's wet winds to rise and drop their rain over India. Not everything is stopped, though. Every spring and autumn, [[@bar-headed-goose|bar-headed geese]] fly right over the range between India and Central Asia.

text: [[echolocation|Echolocation]] means finding things by [[@echoes|listening to echoes]]. A bat flying at night sends out short, loud calls through its mouth or nose. The sound bounces off a moth, a branch or a wall, and the bat's large ears catch the echo.

From that echo, the bat works out how far away something is, how big it is, which way it is moving and even what its surface is like. All this happens in a flash. Most bat calls are [[ultrasound|ultrasound]], pitched too high for human ears. If we could hear them, a summer evening would be surprisingly noisy.

sec.t:
In the 1790s, an Italian scientist named Lazzaro Spallanzani noticed something odd. Bats that could not see still flew around obstacles. But bats with their ears plugged crashed. He could not explain how ears could help a bat "see".

The answer came in the late 1930s. At Harvard University, a student named Donald Griffin brought bats to a physicist who had a machine that could detect ultrasound. Suddenly the silent bats were full of calls. At first, many scientists doubted him. It seemed impossible that a small animal could make such fast judgements from sound. In 1944 Griffin gave the skill its name, echolocation.

Bats tune their calls to where they hunt. Bats that chase insects in open sky use long, lower calls that carry far. Bats that hunt among leaves use short, sharp calls, so the echoes don't blur together. Horseshoe bats call through their noses, and a fleshy, leaf-shaped flap around the nostrils helps focus the sound into a beam, like the light from a torch.

Each kind of bat has its own style of call. Scientists use bat detectors, which turn ultrasound into sounds we can hear, to work out which bats are flying over a park at night. A few birds echolocate too. Swiftlets that nest in dark [[@caves-form|caves]] in the [[@andaman|Andaman Islands]], and oilbirds in South America, find their way with clicks that people can hear.

sec.h: Echoes in water, and in people
sec.t:
Sound travels well underwater, so many toothed whales use it too. [[@dolphins-click|Dolphins]] send clicks through a fatty bump on their forehead. India's national aquatic animal, the Ganges river dolphin, has tiny eyes and lives in muddy water. It depends almost entirely on echolocation to find fish.

Some blind people have taught themselves to do something similar. The American Daniel Kish, blind since he was a baby, clicks his tongue and listens to the echoes. He can ride a bicycle and hike this way, and he teaches others. Ships and [[@submarines|submarines]] use the same idea, called sonar, to measure depth and find objects in the dark sea.

text: Far below the waves, where no sunlight ever reaches, the sea floor has cracks above hot rock. Cold seawater seeps down, gets heated by [[magma|magma]], picks up minerals and gushes back out like an underwater chimney. These places are called hydrothermal vents, and they are crowded with life.

Giant tubeworms as long as a grown-up is tall wave red plumes. White crabs scuttle over the rocks. Clams, mussels, shrimp and pale fish gather in the warm water. None of them depend on sunlight. Their [[foodchain|food chain]] starts with [[bacteria|bacteria]] that turn chemicals from inside the Earth into food.

st.reveal: At 2,500 m down, the water above presses on everything about 250 times harder than air does at the surface. Under that much pressure, water stays liquid far above 100 °C, the same idea that makes a pressure cooker cook faster.

myth: Nothing can live without sunlight.

sec.t:
In 1977, a team of American [[geologist|geologists]] took the small submarine Alvin down about 2,500 m near the [[@galapagos|Galápagos Islands]]. They expected to find hot springs, because the sea floor there is slowly splitting apart over hot, [[@volcano|volcanic]] rock. They did not expect animals.

Instead, their lights showed fields of clams and mussels, and clumps of huge white tubes with blood-red tips. The scientists had brought along equipment for studying rocks, not living things. They had to preserve some of their samples in vodka from the ship's supplies. Two years later, explorers found "black smokers" on the East Pacific Rise, chimneys belching water as black as ink and hot enough to melt lead.

Almost every food chain on Earth starts with plants or [[algae|algae]] capturing sunlight. At vents, it starts with bacteria that use hydrogen sulphide, the gas that smells like rotten eggs, as their energy source. This is called chemosynthesis, meaning "making with chemicals".

Giant tubeworms take this to the extreme. They have no mouth or stomach. Instead, a special organ inside each worm is packed with billions of bacteria. The worm's red plume soaks up chemicals and oxygen from the water, using a kind of [[haemoglobin|haemoglobin]] like the one in your blood. The bacteria do the rest. Tubeworms can grow fast for animals in such a cold, dark world, and a colony can spring up on a new vent within a few years.

Vents do not last forever. A chimney may stop flowing after years or decades, and the animals around it die or move on. Their young drift through the dark water until, with luck, they settle on another vent, sometimes many kilometres away.

{{story:alien-life}}

The vents of the Indian Ocean hold one of the oddest animals on Earth. The scaly-foot snail, found in 2001, builds its shell and the scales on its foot partly from iron sulphide, a metal mineral. It is one of the only animals known to use iron in its skeleton this way.

That metal-rich sea floor has also drawn interest from people. Several countries, including India, hold permits to explore parts of the Indian Ocean floor for minerals. In 2019, the scaly-foot snail became one of the first animals listed as [[endangered|endangered]] because of possible deep-sea mining. Scientists and governments are still debating how to protect vent life while studying these resources.

Vents give scientists a reason to look for life far from Earth. Jupiter's moon [[@europa|Europa]] and Saturn's moon [[@space-weird-oceans-moons|Enceladus]] seem to have salty oceans hidden under thick ice. If those oceans have hot vents too, they might offer the same kind of chemical energy.

Some researchers think life on Earth itself may have begun at deep-sea vents billions of years ago. Others favour shallow pools on land. Nobody knows yet, and the question of how the [[@first-life|first living things]] appeared is still one of the biggest in science.

text: A firework's colours come from metals mixed into small pellets inside it, called stars. Each star contains a fuel, a chemical that provides oxygen, and a metal compound, all packed together.

When the stars burn, they get extremely hot. The heat pumps energy into the metal [[atom|atoms]], pushing their [[electron|electrons]] up to higher energy levels. A moment later, the electrons drop back down and give off that energy as light. Each metal releases light of particular colours. Strontium glows red, barium gives green, copper gives blue, sodium gives yellow and calcium gives orange. Mixing metals makes other shades, like purple from strontium and copper together.
So the colour in the sky is really a glowing signature of the metal inside.

Dyes would simply burn away. The colours come from metal compounds that glow with their own particular colour when they get very hot. Each metal always gives off the same colours, a bit like a fingerprint.

sec.t:
A big display firework is a ball or cylinder called a shell. At the bottom is a lift charge of gunpowder. When it is lit, it shoots the shell out of a tube high into the sky. At the same time, a time fuse starts burning inside.

When the fuse reaches the middle, it lights a burst charge, which breaks the shell open and flings the stars outwards. How the stars are arranged inside decides the shape of the burst: a round flower, a ring, a heart or a smiley face. Some stars change colour as they burn, because they are made in layers, like an onion.

Fireworks are made and set off only by trained experts. They can cause serious burns and eye injuries, so families are always safest watching from a distance.

In India, most fireworks are made in and around [[@made-matchsticks|Sivakasi]] in Tamil Nadu. The hot, dry [[climate|climate]] there helps the chemicals stay dry. Thousands of people work in its factories, many of them preparing for the busy months before [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]].

In the USA, fireworks are a big part of Independence Day on 4 July. Around the world, cities like Sydney, London and Dubai welcome the [[@new-year|new year]] with huge displays timed to music by computers. Each shell is wired to an electric igniter, so a show can fire hundreds of them to the exact beat.

Fireworks leave behind smoke, tiny dust particles and metal compounds. In Delhi and other cities, [[@air-pollution|air pollution]] can rise sharply after Diwali, especially when cold, still weather traps the smoke near the ground. Loud bangs also frighten pets, birds and street animals.

Indian scientists at CSIR-NEERI have developed "green crackers" that aim to produce less smoke and fewer harmful particles. Some places now prefer laser light shows or [[@drones|drone]] shows, where hundreds of glowing drones draw pictures in the sky without any burning at all.

text: A wood carver starts with a solid block and takes away everything that isn't the picture. There is no glue and no paint needed, just sharp tools and patience. A chisel pushed by hand, or tapped with a wooden mallet, lifts off curls of wood. A curved blade called a gouge scoops out hollows. Small knives do the fine work: an eyelid, a feather, a petal.

The hardest part is the grain. Wood is made of long fibres that run up the trunk, like a bundle of drinking straws. Cut along them and the blade glides. Cut against them and the wood splits or tears. So a carver reads each block before touching it, and plans every cut around the way the tree grew.

sec.t:
Saharanpur in Uttar Pradesh is one of India's busiest woodcarving towns. Its workshops turn sheesham, a hard, dark wood, into screens, boxes and furniture covered in vines and leaves. Further south, carvers in [[@mysuru|Mysuru]] work in sandalwood, which is soft enough for tiny detail and keeps its scent for years.

In Kerala, temple ceilings and roof brackets are carved with gods, dancers and elephants. In the old lanes of [[@ahmedabad|Ahmedabad]], many houses have wooden fronts with carved balconies, brackets and doors, some of them a couple of hundred years old. The bright lacquered [[@channapatna-toys|Channapatna toys]] of Karnataka start life on a lathe, a machine that spins the wood while a blade shapes it.

sec.h: Poles that tell a family story
sec.t:
On the Pacific coast of Canada and Alaska, the Haida, Tlingit and other nations carve totem poles from western red cedar. A tall pole can take a team months. The figures, such as ravens, bears, whales and eagles, stand for clans, family histories and important events. Some poles welcome visitors. Others honour someone who has died.

Totem poles are not idols and were never worshipped. They work more like a carved family record. After a ban in Canada was lifted in 1951, carvers revived the art, and new poles are still raised today with feasts and speeches.

Carvers choose wood the way cooks choose flour. Lime and basswood are soft, pale and even, which is why many beginners in Europe and the USA start with them. Walnut and teak are tougher and show a beautiful grain. Rosewood is dense and almost black.

Sandalwood and boxwood allow very fine detail. Pine is cheap but its knots and uneven rings can make a blade jump.

Carvers also watch moisture. Wet, freshly cut "green" wood carves easily but can crack as it dries. That's why many traditional carvers store their logs for months, sometimes years, before the first cut.

Painters can paint over a mistake. A carver can't put wood back. That makes carving a slow, careful art, where a single slip can ruin weeks of work. It also explains why masters in Saharanpur or Kerala often learned from a parent, starting as children with simple leaves before moving on to faces.

text: A national anthem is a song that stands for a country. It is played at official ceremonies, sports matches, school assemblies and when leaders visit other nations. When people sing it together, it reminds them that they belong to the same country, whatever language they speak at home.

Most anthems are short and easy to sing in a crowd. They usually praise the land, remember a struggle for freedom, or ask for blessings on the nation. Many became anthems long after they were written, because people already loved them. A few were written to order, for a competition or a new [[constitution|constitution]], and some countries have swapped one anthem for another.

myth: Jana Gana Mana was written to praise King George V.

This rumour began because the song was first sung in December 1911, during the King's visit to India. Tagore himself denied it in a letter years later, saying the "dispenser of India's destiny" in the song was not any king.

sec.t:
*Jana Gana Mana* was written by Rabindranath [[@tagore|Tagore]] in [[@bengali-language|Bengali]], in a style rich in Sanskrit words, so it can be understood across much of India. It was first sung on 27 December 1911 at a session of the Indian National Congress in Calcutta. The song names regions, rivers and mountains from across the country, from Punjab and Sindh to Bengal, and from the Himalaya to the seas.

The [[@constituent-assembly|Constituent Assembly]] adopted its first stanza as the national anthem on 24 January 1950, two days before [[@constitution|the Constitution]] came into force. The full version takes about 52 seconds.

{{story:tagore}}

Tagore also wrote *Amar Shonar Bangla*, which became the national anthem of [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]] in 1971. Very few people in history have written the national anthems of two countries.

*The Star-Spangled Banner* began as a poem by Francis Scott Key. In 1814, during a war with Britain, he watched British ships bombard Fort McHenry in Baltimore through the night. At dawn, he saw a huge American flag still flying, and wrote about it. His words were set to a popular British tune. The song became the official US anthem only in 1931.

It is famously hard to sing. Its melody spans about an [[octave|octave]] and a half, a wide range for most voices, and singers at big games sometimes crack on the high notes. The flag Key saw still exists and hangs in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History.

The Netherlands' anthem, *Het Wilhelmus*, has a tune and words from the 1500s, which makes it one of the oldest. Japan's anthem, *Kimigayo*, has words from a poem more than a thousand years old, and it is one of the shortest anywhere. Britain's *God Save the King* changes to "Queen" when a queen is on the throne. Spain's *Marcha Real* has no official words at all.

Some countries have changed their anthems after big changes in history. [[@south-africa|South Africa]]'s anthem, adopted after the end of [[@apartheid|apartheid]], mixes five of the country's languages in a single song.

In India, people stand to attention when the anthem is played. In 1986, the Supreme Court considered the case of three schoolchildren in Kerala who had been expelled for not singing it because of their religious beliefs. They had stood respectfully. The Court ruled that they could not be punished for staying silent while standing.

In 2016, the Supreme Court ordered cinemas to play the anthem before films. In 2018, it changed that order, making it optional. Anthems carry strong feelings, which is why rules about them are argued over so often. Like [[@flags|flags]], they are simple things that can mean a great deal.

text: The crossword was invented by Arthur Wynne, a journalist from Liverpool who had moved to the United States. On 21 December 1913, he needed a new puzzle for the Christmas edition of the *New York World*'s Sunday fun section. He drew a diamond-shaped grid, wrote a list of clues and called it a "word-cross".

A few weeks later, a typesetting slip swapped the words, and "cross-word" stuck. Within about ten years, the puzzle had spread across America and to Britain, and soon to newspapers all over the world, including India.

st.prompt: What shape was the very first crossword puzzle in 1913?

A perfect 15-by-15 square
A circle like a clock face

st.reveal: Arthur Wynne's word-cross was diamond-shaped, with an empty space in the middle. It had no black squares at all. The square grids with black squares came a few years later.

myth: Crosswords are an ancient puzzle, as old as word games themselves.
Word squares, where words read the same across and down, go back to Roman times. But the crossword with clues and a grid of crossing answers was invented in 1913 by Arthur Wynne.

sec.t:
Wynne's grid had no black squares. The words simply crossed in a diamond around an empty middle. The very first clue was "What bargain hunters enjoy", and the answer was SALES. Most clues were simple, though one asked for "the fibre of the gomuti palm". The answer was DOH, which hardly anyone knew.

Readers wrote in asking for more. Wynne kept making them, and soon readers were sending in their own puzzles too. The grids changed shape over the next few years, from diamonds to squares, and black squares appeared to separate the words.

Most modern American crosswords follow neat rules. The grid is usually 15 squares by 15 on weekdays. Every white square belongs to two words, one across and one down. The pattern of black squares looks the same if you turn the grid upside down. That's called rotational [[@symmetry|symmetry]].

The setter usually starts with a few long theme answers, then fills the gaps. This is the hard part. Each new word has to fit letters already placed, which is a bit like building a tower of cards where every card touches four others. Many setters now use computer word lists to help, though the clues are still written by people.

British newspapers developed the cryptic crossword, where each clue is a little riddle. A clue might hide the answer inside other words, or scramble letters in an anagram. For example, "Silent, mixed up, will pay attention (6)" points to LISTEN, because the letters of SILENT can be rearranged into it.

Indian English newspapers, such as *The Hindu*, have run cryptic crosswords for decades, and puzzles also appear in Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and other languages. A crossword in Hindi is trickier than it looks, because one letter of Devanagari can carry a vowel sign too.

A crossword gives you small wins, one word at a time, and each answer helps with the next. Puzzles like [[@sudoku|sudoku]] work in a similar way with numbers. Solvers also pick up odd words: setters love short words full of vowels, like ERA, ALOE and OREO.

Researchers have studied whether [[@puzzles-logic|puzzles]] protect the brain as people age. The results are mixed. Puzzles certainly make people better at puzzles, and that alone has kept crosswords in [[@newspapers|newspapers]] for more than a hundred years.

text: Sports science uses biology, physics, chemistry and psychology to help athletes train better, perform better and stay healthy. Scientists measure how hearts, [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] and [[@muscles|muscles]] respond to training. They film movements with fast cameras, design better equipment and study [[@sports-nutrition|food]], sleep and the mind.
Small gains add up. In top sport, the gap between first and fourth can be one hundredth of a second, so anything that helps a little can matter a lot.

options.t: It makes more red blood cells to carry oxygen
It makes the lungs grow bigger
It makes muscles lighter

st.reveal: Air high up has less oxygen in each breath, so over a few weeks the body makes more red blood cells. When athletes return to lower ground, their blood can carry oxygen more easily.

myth: Stretching before exercise prevents injuries.

Studies suggest that holding long stretches before exercise does little to prevent injury and may slightly reduce power. Experts recommend a gentle warm-up that gets you moving, such as jogging and swinging your arms and legs.

sec.t:
Sports scientists track how hard an athlete is working. Heart-rate monitors show how fast the [[@heartbeat-exercise|heart]] beats during training. Lab tests measure VO2 max, the most oxygen the body can use in a minute, which shows how fit a runner or cyclist is.

Coaches use these numbers to plan training so athletes push hard on some days and recover on others. Too little rest leads to injury and tiredness. That is why many teams now treat [[@sleep-why|sleep]] as part of training.

Nutritionists plan meals so athletes get enough energy before hard sessions and enough [[protein|protein]] to repair muscles afterwards. Sports psychologists help athletes handle nerves. One common method is visualisation, rehearsing a race or a penalty kick in the mind before doing it for real.

Sometimes science changes a whole technique. In the 1960s, [[@sport-science-high-jump|Dick Fosbury]] of the USA started high-jumping backwards, head first, arching his back over the bar. Soft foam landing mats made this safe. He won gold at the 1968 Olympics in [[@mexico|Mexico]] City.

The Fosbury Flop works partly because the athlete's [[centre-of-mass|centre of mass]], the balance point of the body, can pass just under the bar while the arched body goes over it. Almost every top high-jumper now uses it.

For years, people wondered whether anyone could run a mile, about 1.6 km, in under four minutes. Roger Bannister, a British medical student, studied his own breathing and training in the lab.

On 6 May 1954, on a track in Oxford, he ran 3 minutes 59.4 seconds, helped by friends who took turns setting the pace. Within weeks someone else had run faster. Today pacemakers are used in races, including record attempts in the [[@running-marathon|marathon]].

Since about 2017, [[@sport-science-shoes|running shoes]] with thick foam and a carbon plate have helped runners save energy. In early lab tests, runners used about 4% less energy in them. Records tumbled, and World Athletics introduced limits on how thick soles can be.

Not all help is allowed. Some athletes have cheated by taking banned drugs that build muscle or add red blood cells. The World Anti-Doping Agency, set up in 1999, tests athletes and keeps a list of banned substances.

In India, the Sports Authority of India runs centres where scientists work with athletes. The best advice from all this research is simple enough for anyone: train regularly, eat well, drink water and sleep enough.

text: Usain Bolt is the fastest person ever timed. In 2009, at the World Championships in Berlin, he ran 100 metres in 9.58 seconds and 200 metres in 19.19 seconds. Both are still [[@world-records|world records]].

His average [[@speed-distance|speed]] in that 100 metres was about 37.6 km/h. Between the 60-metre and 80-metre marks, he reached about 44 km/h. That is roughly the speed of a car on a city road. A [[@fastest-animal|cheetah]] is much faster, but [[@body-speed-limit|no human has run as fast as Bolt]] over that stretch.

It is worth remembering how short a 100-metre race is. It is a little shorter than a football field, and about five times the length of a cricket pitch. Bolt covered it in less time than it takes most people to tie a shoelace.

st.reveal: Bolt took about 41 strides, each roughly 2.4 metres long. Most of his rivals needed about 44 or 45. His long legs meant fewer steps, while he still moved them very quickly.

Bolt was often slow out of the blocks, but his long stride made up for it later in the race. He showed that being tall can be an advantage once a sprinter gets moving.

sec.t:
Bolt was born in 1986 in Sherwood Content, a small village in Trelawny, Jamaica. As a boy he loved [[@cricket-history|cricket]] and wanted to be a fast bowler. A cricket coach at school noticed how fast he ran and suggested he try athletics.

By 15 he was winning the 200 metres at the World Junior Championships in Kingston, in front of a home crowd. He was so nervous before the race that he put his shoes on the wrong feet, according to his own account. He won anyway.

At the 2008 Beijing Olympics, Bolt won the 100 metres in a world record of 9.69 seconds, even though he slowed down to celebrate before the line. He also won the 200 metres in a world record.

He won both races again in London in 2012 and in Rio in 2016. No one else has won the Olympic 100 and 200 metres at three Games in a row. Fans copied his famous pose, an arm pointing up at the sky like a bolt of lightning.

Bolt also won relay golds with the Jamaican team. In 2017, one of his 2008 relay teammates was found to have used a banned substance, and the team lost that gold medal. Bolt himself was never found to have cheated, but he had to give back the medal. That left him with eight Olympic golds.

He also had scoliosis, a curve in the spine. He worked on strengthening the muscles around his back and hips to protect it.

Bolt retired after the 2017 World Championships in London. In his last race, a relay, he pulled up with a hamstring injury and fell to the track. It was a sad finish, but the crowd cheered him anyway.

After athletics he trained briefly with a professional football club in Australia. His records still stand more than fifteen years later. Some scientists think humans can go a little faster, perhaps under 9.5 seconds one day, but nobody knows for sure.

text: Screens affect your body in two main ways: through your eyes and through your sleep.

When you look at a screen up close for a long time, the tiny [[@muscles|muscles]] inside your eyes work hard to keep it in focus, and you blink much less. Your eyes can get tired, dry, itchy or blurry for a while. This is called digital eye strain. It goes away with rest. Screens also give off bright light, and bright light in the evening tells your brain it's still daytime. That can delay the [[hormone|hormone]] that makes you sleepy. Exciting games and videos keep your brain alert too. So screen use late at night can push bedtime later and make sleep shorter.

st.prompt: In Taiwan, schools started sending children outside for longer each day. What happened to the number of short-sighted children?

options.t: It went down
It went up
It stayed exactly the same

st.reveal: Many studies have found that children who spend more time outdoors are less likely to become short-sighted. After Taiwan encouraged two hours of outdoor time a day from 2010, the rise in short sight among schoolchildren reversed.

myth: Sitting close to the TV will ruin your eyesight.

Sitting close may tire your eyes, but it doesn't damage them. Children often sit close because they can focus up close more easily than adults. If a child must sit close to see clearly, though, it can be a sign they need glasses.

sec.t:
To see something close, a ring of muscle inside each eye squeezes to change the shape of the lens. Reading a book needs it too, but people tend to stare at screens for longer without a break. Your eyes also blink less when you concentrate, sometimes half as often as normal. Each blink spreads [[@gross-eye-boogers|a fresh layer of tears]], so fewer [[@blinking|blinks]] mean drier eyes.

Eye doctors in the USA suggest the 20-20-20 rule. Every 20 minutes, look at something about 6 metres away for 20 seconds. That relaxes the focusing muscles. Keeping the screen at arm's length helps too.

Your body has an inner clock that follows light and dark. As evening comes, your brain releases melatonin, a hormone that helps you feel sleepy. Bright light, especially bluish light, can delay it. Phones, tablets and laptops give off quite a lot of blue light, and we hold them close to our faces.

Yet scientists think blue light is only part of the story. A gripping game, a funny video or messages from friends keep your brain switched on, whatever the colour of the light. Many sleep experts suggest putting screens away about an hour before bed and keeping phones out of the bedroom at night. [[@sleep-why|Sleep]] matters a lot for growing children, for memory and for mood.

Glasses that filter blue light are sold widely in India and the USA. In 2023, a large review of studies found little evidence that they reduce eye strain or improve sleep. Eye doctors generally don't recommend them for this.

Screens can be great for learning, staying in touch and having fun. The trick is balance: breaks for your eyes, time outside, screens off before bed. [[@smartphones|Smartphones]] and computers have made screens part of daily life, so families often agree simple rules that suit them. Knowing how to stay [[@online-safety|safe online]] matters as much as caring for your eyes.

text: A digital camera turns light into a grid of tiny squares called [[@pixels|pixels]]. Each [[pixel|pixel]] is stored as numbers: how much red, green and blue it has. So to a computer, a photo is a giant table of numbers. Computer vision is the skill of finding meaning in those numbers, such as "this is a face", "that is a zebra crossing" or "this leaf has a disease".

Today, most computer vision uses [[@neural-networks|neural networks]], programs that learn by looking at millions of labelled pictures. They are not given rules for what a cat looks like. They work the rules out from examples.

Fill in your grid from the numbers and see how long it takes to guess the picture. That is close to how a computer starts.

A computer starts with a grid of numbers, one set for each pixel. Any idea of "dog" or "road" is something it has to learn by finding patterns in those numbers, after training on many labelled examples.

sec.t:
The big change came from two things: lots of data and much faster computers. Starting in 2009, a team led by Fei-Fei Li at Stanford built ImageNet, a collection of about 14 million pictures labelled by people with words like "goldfish" or "fire engine".

In 2012, a neural network called AlexNet entered the ImageNet contest and made far fewer mistakes than any program before it. Its layers learned step by step. The first layers spotted edges and blobs of colour. Middle layers put those together into shapes like eyes or wheels. The last layers recognised whole things. Since then, programs have become better than most people at certain narrow picture tasks.

Your phone may open when it sees your face, after comparing it with a map of your features it stored when you set it up. At several Indian airports, the DigiYatra system lets passengers walk through gates using [[@face-recognition|face recognition]] instead of showing a boarding pass. Apps can name a bird or a plant from a photo. [[@self-driving|Self-driving]] cars use cameras to read lanes, signs and people crossing.

Doctors use it too. Some programs help check eye scans for damage caused by diabetes, or spot shadows on chest X-rays that a busy doctor might miss. Farmers point phones at crops to identify pests. In each case, the computer is very good at one job and knows nothing outside it.

Computer vision can fail in strange ways. In a 2017 study, researchers placed a few stickers on a STOP sign, and an image-recognition system read it as a speed limit sign. A person would never make that mistake. Other programs have labelled a picture of a cow on a beach wrongly, because in their training photos, cows always stood on grass.

Face recognition has also made more mistakes with some groups of people than others, especially when its training pictures didn't include enough variety. That has led to arguments about privacy, fairness and when such systems should be allowed. Engineers are working on these problems, but seeing like a human, with common sense about the world, is still out of reach.

text: A hearing aid is a tiny amplifier you wear in or behind the ear. A microphone picks up sound, a small computer chip boosts the [[frequency|frequencies]] the person struggles to hear, and a tiny speaker plays the sound into the ear canal. It helps people whose ears still work but have become less sensitive.

A cochlear implant is for people whose inner ear is badly damaged. Instead of making sound louder, it changes sound into electrical pulses. A thin strip of electrodes, placed by a [[surgeon|surgeon]] inside the spiral-shaped [[cochlea|cochlea]], sends those pulses straight to the hearing [[nerve|nerve]]. The brain learns to understand them as sound.

Makes sounds even louder than a hearing aid

myth: Hearing aids give people back perfect, normal hearing, like glasses do for eyes.
Hearing aids help a lot, but they can't repair damaged parts of the ear. Sounds may seem different at first, and noisy places can still be hard. The brain needs time to get used to them.

sec.t:
When [[@sound-travel|sound]] enters your [[@ears-hear|ear]], it shakes the eardrum, which passes the [[vibration|vibration]] through three tiny bones to the cochlea. Inside the cochlea are thousands of tiny hair cells. Each responds to a different pitch: those at the wide end to high sounds, those deep in the spiral to low ones. When they bend, they fire signals along the hearing nerve to the brain.

Loud noise, [[@ageing|ageing]], some illnesses and some medicines can damage these hair cells. Once lost, they don't grow back in humans. A hearing aid helps the survivors work harder. When too few are left, a cochlear implant takes over their job.

An implant has two parts. Outside, a sound processor sits behind the ear with a microphone. It turns sounds into a code and sends it through the skin by radio to the inside part, which is held in place by a magnet.

Inside, under the skin, a receiver passes the code to a strip of up to about two dozen electrodes curled through the cochlea. Each electrode stimulates nerve fibres for a different pitch, copying the way hair cells are laid out. The Australian surgeon Graeme Clark and his team implanted their first multichannel device in 1978. By 2019, the US National Institutes of Health estimated about 737,000 implants worldwide.

At first, an implant can sound strange: beeps, buzzes or robot voices. With practice, the brain learns to make sense of it. Young children who get implants early, often around their first birthday, can learn to speak and understand speech well. In India, a government scheme helps pay for implants for young children from families who can't afford them.

Not everyone who is deaf wants to hear. Many Deaf people, who often write "Deaf" with a capital D, see themselves as a community with its own culture and its own [[@sign-language|sign language]], not as people with something to fix. Some have worried that implants push children away from signing. Others feel implants open doors. Today, many families choose both: an implant and sign language.

The World Health Organization says more than 1.5 billion people live with some hearing loss, and many could be helped by a hearing aid but don't have one. In many places, the biggest gap is not the technology but the cost and the lack of hearing tests.

text: Several of the world's biggest technology companies are run by people who grew up in India. Sundar Pichai leads Google and its parent company Alphabet. Satya Nadella leads Microsoft. Shantanu Narayen has led Adobe since 2007 and is handing over in December 2026 to Anil Chakravarthy, another IIT graduate. Arvind Krishna leads IBM. Many more Indian-born engineers run teams and start companies in [[@silicon-valley|Silicon Valley]].

There isn't one simple reason. Experts point to a mix: India's strong engineering colleges, the English language, a culture that prizes education, and United States immigration rules that welcomed highly educated engineers. Timing mattered too. These leaders arrived just as the computer and internet industries were growing fastest.

sec.h: Schools built for a new nation
sec.t:
After independence in 1947, Prime Minister [[@nehru|Jawaharlal Nehru]] wanted India to train its own scientists and engineers. The first Indian Institute of Technology opened in 1951 at Kharagpur in West Bengal, in a building where the British had once imprisoned freedom fighters. More IITs followed in Bombay, Madras, Kanpur and Delhi.

Entry was fiercely competitive, and still is. Each year more than a million students sit the main engineering entrance test, and only a small share get IIT seats. Graduates were very well trained in maths and engineering. Sundar Pichai studied at IIT Kharagpur. Satya Nadella studied at Manipal, in [[@karnataka|Karnataka]].

Sundar Pichai grew up in [[@chennai|Chennai]], where his father was an electrical engineer and his mother had worked as a stenographer. He has said his family didn't get a telephone until he was about 12, and he remembered phone numbers easily. He went to Stanford University on a scholarship, joined Google in 2004, and became its chief executive in 2015.

Satya Nadella grew up in [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]], loved cricket and studied electrical engineering before moving to the United States. He joined Microsoft in 1992 and became its chief executive in 2014.

Once a few Indians reached top jobs, they helped others. Indian engineers formed groups to support each other, share advice and invest in each other's startups.

There's also what scientists call selection. The Indians who moved to America were not typical Indians. They were mostly those who had won places at top colleges and could pass strict visa rules. So their success says more about education and opportunity than about Indians in general. Indian Americans now have one of the highest average household incomes of any group in the United States, which reflects this careful selection.

For decades, people in India worried about "brain drain": the country paid to train engineers, who then left. Others now talk of "brain circulation". Many engineers have returned to India to start companies, and India receives more money sent home by workers abroad than any other country. India's own tech giants, such as TCS, Infosys and Wipro, grew into [[@global-companies|global companies]], and many of India's [[@indian-startups|startups]] were founded by people who once worked in the United States.

text: The best-known floating post office sits on Dal Lake in Srinagar, Kashmir. It is a wooden houseboat moored near Nehru Park, painted and carved like the other houseboats on the lake. Inside, staff sell stamps, accept parcels, send speed post and help people with savings forms, like any Indian post office.

Customers often arrive by *shikara*, the slim, canopied boats of Dal Lake. Letters posted there can get a special postmark showing a shikara and boatman, which makes it a favourite with tourists and stamp collectors. A second floating post office, on a boat in Detroit, USA, delivers letters to ships as they sail past. Both are working post offices. They are not museums or tourist props, and they handle real letters every day.

st.prompt: How does Detroit's floating post office hand mail to big ships on the river?

It fires the letters across with a cannon

st.reveal: The little mail boat steers right up beside huge cargo ships while they keep moving. Crew on deck lower a bucket on a rope, and the mail goes up in it. Ships' crews have been getting letters this way since 1895.

sec.h: A post office on the water
sec.t:
Dal Lake is a neighbourhood as well as a view. Thousands of people live on and around it, on houseboats and on small islands with floating vegetable gardens. For them, getting to the city post office meant a boat trip.

News reports say a postal boat began serving lake residents in 1953. The houseboat post office grew from that service. In 2011, the head of the postal circle gave it its current name, the Floating Post Office, and it became a tourist attraction too.

In 2014, huge floods hit Kashmir. The houseboat was damaged and drifted from its place, and much of a small stamp museum inside was lost. It was repaired and opened again. Today it has a little display of old stamps and the history of mail in [[@kashmir|Kashmir]].

The post office has only a few staff. Mail collected during the day goes to Srinagar's main post office, then on across India.

The houseboat looks much like its neighbours on Dal Lake, with carved wooden panels and a long, flat hull. The post office counter is at one end, and the little display of stamps is at the other. People who live on the lake still come by shikara to send money orders, pay bills and pick up parcels, just as they would at any post office on land. Visitors take off their shoes before stepping in, as they would in a home.

{{story:oddity-hindustani-mail}}

Halfway round the world, the Detroit River links two of the [[@great-lakes|Great Lakes]] and is one of the busiest shipping lanes in North America. Huge cargo ships, some longer than two football fields, pass day and night.

Since 1895, a company has carried mail out to these ships by boat. Today its small mail boat, the *J. W. Westcott II*, is a real US post office with its own ZIP code, 48222. It pulls up beside a moving freighter, crew on deck lower a bucket on a rope, and the mail goes up. Sailors who spend months on the lakes can get letters, parcels and supplies this way without their ships stopping.

A postmark is the ink mark printed over a stamp to show it has been used. Most just give the town and date. Special postmarks with pictures, called pictorial cancellations, are made for unusual places and events. India Post uses them at several famous sites, and the Dal Lake shikara design is among the most popular.

Collectors love these little ink pictures, and many travel to Srinagar partly to get one. For an Indian collector, the biggest prize is a copy of the very [[@hist-first-stamp-india|first stamp]] issued in the [[subcontinent|subcontinent]], in 1852, which is far rarer than any floating postmark.

text: The shortest war on record was fought between Britain and Zanzibar, an island state off the coast of East Africa, on 27 August 1896. It began a little after nine in the morning and was over in roughly 40 minutes. Accounts from the time differ slightly, so you will see anything from 38 to 45 minutes.

The war was about who would rule Zanzibar. When a new sultan took the throne without Britain's approval, British warships opened fire on his palace. It was a lopsided fight. Britain had five warships and hundreds of marines and sailors. Zanzibar had a few old cannons, a palace made largely of wood and one small armed ship. The palace was soon in ruins and the new sultan had fled.

st.prompt: What finally ended the Anglo-Zanzibar War?

options.t: A peace treaty signed after long talks
The palace flag was shot down and the guns fell silent
A storm forced the British ships to leave

st.reveal: After about 40 minutes of shelling, the palace was in ruins and its flag was brought down. The new sultan had already fled, and the firing stopped. No treaty or talks were needed.

n.certNote: Everyone agrees the war lasted well under an hour. Accounts written at the time give slightly different start and end times, so you will see figures from about 38 to 45 minutes.

sec.h: An island of cloves and trade
sec.t:
Zanzibar was a rich place. Its farms grew huge amounts of cloves, and for a time it was the world's leading producer of the [[@spices|spice]]. Ships rode the [[monsoon|monsoon]] winds between Zanzibar, Arabia and India, carrying ivory, cloth and spices along old [[@trade-routes|trade routes]].

Indian merchants from Gujarat and Kutch lived there in large numbers. The Indian rupee was used as money on the island. Zanzibar was also a centre of the East African slave trade, which Britain was trying to end. By the 1890s, Britain treated the sultanate as a protectorate and expected a say in who ruled it.

sec.h: A sultan who would not step down

sec.t:
Khalid did not leave. At about 9:02, the ships opened fire. The wooden palace was badly damaged within minutes and caught fire. Zanzibar's only real warship, a former royal yacht called HHS Glasgow, fired back with small guns and was sunk where it lay. Its crew raised a British flag to show they had given up.

By around 9:40 the palace flag was down and the guns went quiet. Khalid had already slipped away and found shelter in the German consulate. The masts of the sunken Glasgow poked out of the harbour water for years afterwards.

Britain put Hamud bin Muhammed on the throne that same day. The following year, under British pressure, he issued a decree abolishing slavery on the islands. The story of how that cruel trade ended is told in [[@slavery-freedom|slavery and freedom]].

Khalid escaped to German East Africa on the mainland. British forces captured him there during the First World War, about 20 years later. He was sent into exile and later allowed to return to East Africa, where he died in 1927.

The war is famous mainly for being so short. It also shows how the great powers of the 1890s used gunboats to decide who ruled smaller states. Zanzibar stayed under British protection until 1963, then joined the mainland country of Tanganyika in 1964 to form Tanzania.

Today Stone Town, the old heart of Zanzibar City, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with carved wooden doors that show Indian, Arab and African styles side by side. From its harbour on a clear day, you look towards the coast where, further north, Kenya's grasslands begin the [[@kenya-safari|great safari country]] of East Africa.

text: Australia has been an island for tens of millions of years. Long ago it was part of a giant southern landmass called [[gondwana|Gondwana]], joined to [[@antarctica|Antarctica]], South America and India. Over time those lands drifted apart, and Australia finally broke away from Antarctica and floated north on its own.

Cut off from the rest of the world, its animals went their own way. Elsewhere, [[mammal|mammals]] whose babies grow inside the mother for a long time took over. In Australia, [[marsupial|marsupials]], whose tiny babies finish growing in a pouch, filled almost every job instead: grazing, climbing, burrowing and hunting.

They are born live, like puppies

st.reveal: A mother platypus lays one to three small, soft eggs in a burrow. After the babies hatch, she feeds them milk that oozes from patches on her skin, because she has no nipples.

myth: Sydney is the capital of Australia.
The capital is Canberra. It was built from scratch as a compromise in the early 1900s, because Sydney and Melbourne each wanted the honour and neither would let the other have it.

sec.t:
A newborn kangaroo, called a joey, is about the size of a jelly bean. It crawls through its mother's fur into her pouch and stays there for months. Koalas, [[@wild-wombat-cubes|wombats]] and Tasmanian devils are marsupials too.

Koalas eat almost nothing but eucalyptus (gum) leaves, which are tough and mildly poisonous to most animals. Their slow [[digestion|digestion]] and low-energy diet are why koalas sleep 18 hours a day or more. Then there are the monotremes, the platypus and the echidna, which lay eggs. The platypus also hunts with its bill, sensing tiny electrical signals from shrimps and worms in muddy water with its eyes and ears shut.

Australia is famous for venomous animals. The inland taipan has the most powerful [[venom|venom]] of any land snake tested in the lab. There are box jellyfish in its northern seas and funnel-web spiders in Sydney's gardens.

The real risk is smaller than the reputation. Good antivenoms, quick hospitals and careful habits mean deaths are rare.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived in Australia for at least 50,000 years, one of the longest continuous cultures on Earth. To reach it, their ancestors had to cross open sea from Southeast Asia, among the earliest long sea journeys we know of.

They knew the land intimately: which plants could be eaten, where water hid in the desert and how to manage the bush with careful burning. [[@uluru|Uluru]], the giant red rock in the middle of the country, is a sacred site for its traditional owners, the Anangu. Since 2019, visitors have no longer been allowed to climb it.

Australia and India are on opposite sides of the Indian Ocean but share some big passions. [[@cricket-history|Cricket]] is the most obvious. India and Australia play some of the fiercest Test series in the sport, and both countries have won the men's World Cup several times.

Many Indians now live, study and work in Australia, especially in Melbourne and Sydney. Hindi and [[@punjabi-gurmukhi|Punjabi]] are among the fastest-growing languages spoken at home there. Off its north-east coast lies the [[@great-barrier-reef|Great Barrier Reef]], the largest [[@coral-reefs|coral reef]] system on Earth, which stretches for about 2,300 km.

text: Jerusalem is an ancient city in the hills between the Mediterranean Sea and the [[@dead-sea|Dead Sea]]. Its walled Old City is smaller than a square kilometre, yet it holds sacred places for three of the world's great [[@religions-world|religions]]. For Jews, it is the site of the ancient Temple and the holiest city on Earth. For Christians, it is where Jesus taught, died and, they believe, rose from the dead. For Muslims, it is the third holiest city after Mecca and Medina.

Because so many people care so deeply about it, Jerusalem has been fought over many times. Today, both Israelis and Palestinians see it as their capital, and its future is one of the hardest questions in world politics.

st.reveal: The Temple stood on a huge raised platform. The Western Wall is part of the massive wall built to hold up that platform, more than 2,000 years ago. It is the closest place to the site of the Temple where Jews have been able to pray for most of history.

n.certNote: Each faith tells the city's early history in its own way, and archaeologists still debate some of it. The city's political status is also disputed. This article describes what different groups believe without taking sides.

The Temple was destroyed by the Romans in 70 CE. The Western Wall is part of the huge retaining wall built around the platform the Temple stood on.

sec.t:
Jewish tradition says [[@ancient-israel|King David]] made Jerusalem his capital about 3,000 years ago, and his son Solomon built the first Temple. A second Temple later stood on a vast stone platform. In 70 CE, the armies of [[@ancient-rome|ancient Rome]] destroyed it.

A section of the huge wall that held up the platform survives. It is called the Western Wall, or the Kotel. Jews from all over the world come to pray there. Many write prayers on small slips of paper and tuck them into the cracks between the giant stones. Twice a year the notes are gathered and buried respectfully on the Mount of Olives nearby.

sec.h: The Dome of the Rock and Al-Aqsa

sec.t:
A short walk away is the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Many Christians believe it was built over the place where Jesus was crucified and buried. Several Christian groups share the building, and they have strict rules about who looks after which corner, which lamps and even which steps.

To keep the peace between them, the church door has for centuries been opened each morning by members of Muslim families. One family keeps the large iron key, another opens the door. It is a small daily [[ritual|ritual]] in a city where neighbours of different faiths have often found ways to share space.

sec.h: Walls, stone and a disputed future
sec.t:
The walls around the Old City were built in the 1530s by the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. Inside are four quarters, Jewish, Christian, Muslim and Armenian, packed with narrow lanes, markets and homes. Under a rule dating from British times, new buildings are faced with pale local limestone, so the whole city glows gold at sunset.

Israel controls the whole city and calls it its capital. Palestinians want East Jerusalem, which includes the Old City, as the capital of a future Palestinian state. Most countries keep their embassies in Tel Aviv while the question is unresolved, though the USA moved its embassy to Jerusalem in 2018.

text: Charles Dickens was an English novelist who lived from 1812 to 1870. He wrote Oliver Twist, A Christmas Carol, David Copperfield, Great Expectations and many more. In his lifetime he was the most popular writer in the English-speaking world, and people queued to buy each new instalment of his stories.

Dickens wrote about [[@london|London]] in the time of the [[@industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]], when the city was crowded, smoky and unfair to the poor. He created hundreds of unforgettable characters, from the miser Scrooge to the pickpocket the Artful Dodger. His stories are funny and sad at once, and they made readers angry about cruelty to children.

st.reveal: Readers bought each new part for a small price and waited for the next one. Dickens often wrote just ahead of his readers, and he could change a story if sales went up or down. Radio didn't exist until long after his death.

sec.h: The boy in the blacking factory
sec.t:
When Charles was twelve, his father was sent to the Marshalsea, a prison for people who could not pay their debts. Much of the family went with him, as was common then. Charles was sent to work at Warren's Blacking, a factory near the River Thames. For about ten hours a day he pasted labels on pots of boot polish.

He worked there for about a year, but he never forgot the shame and loneliness. He kept it secret for most of his life, even from his own children. Many of his books are about children who are abandoned, overworked or treated badly.

In 1843, short of money, Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in about six weeks. It tells of Ebenezer Scrooge, a mean old businessman visited by [[@ghost-stories|three ghosts]] on Christmas Eve, who wakes up a kinder man.

The book was an instant hit. It helped make [[@christmas|Christmas]] in Britain and America a festival of family, feasting and giving to the poor. Scrooge's name became an everyday word for a stingy person, and the story has been filmed dozens of times, once with the Muppets.

Dickens used his fame to campaign. He visited schools, prisons and workhouses, and wrote about what he saw in his novels and magazine articles. He supported a home for homeless women and spoke up for education for poor children. Britain later passed laws limiting [[@rights-kids|child labour]] and making schooling compulsory, and many readers felt Dickens had helped change attitudes.

He was not a perfect man. He separated from his wife, Catherine, in 1858 and treated her unkindly in public. Some of his characters, like Fagin in Oliver Twist, are now seen as unfair stereotypes, and he changed parts of that book after a reader complained.

He visited America twice. On the second trip, in 1867 and 1868, he gave hugely popular public readings, acting out all the voices. When he died in 1870, he was buried in Westminster Abbey, in a corner reserved for writers called Poets' Corner. His last novel, The Mystery of Edwin Drood, was left half-written, and nobody knows how he planned to end it.

text: People in the same country speak differently because languages are always changing, and they change in different ways in different places. Mountains, rivers, distance and old borders kept groups apart for centuries. Each group's speech slowly drifted in its own direction.

These local versions of a language are called [[dialect|dialects]]. They have their own words, sounds and sometimes [[@grammar-why|grammar]]. A person from Bihar and a person from Haryana might both speak Hindi but choose different words for the same things. A Texan and a New Yorker can tell where the other grew up within a sentence.

Pop

st.reveal: In many southern states, "coke" can mean any soft drink. A waiter may ask "What kind of coke?" and you could answer "lemonade". "Pop" is common in the Midwest and Northwest, and "soda" in the Northeast and California.

sec.t:
Picture a group of people who all speak the same way. Some move over a mountain range and lose touch with the rest. Every generation, small changes creep in: a vowel shifts, a new word is borrowed, an old one is forgotten. After a few hundred years, the two groups sound noticeably different.

Contact with other languages matters too. Near borders, people borrow words from their neighbours. In US cities, immigrants from Ireland, Italy, Germany, Mexico and elsewhere left traces in local English. That is part of the [[@immigration-stories|story of immigration]] in America.

Before cars, trains and television, most people spent their whole lives within a small area. So speech could change from one cluster of villages to the next, just as the Hindi saying about every four kos says. A kos is an old unit of distance of roughly 3 km.

Linguists use "accent" for the way words sound, and "dialect" for a whole package of sounds, words and grammar. Everyone has an accent, even people who think they don't.

The line between a dialect and a separate language is blurry. Spoken Hindi and Urdu are so close that speakers understand each other easily, but they use different scripts and literary words, and are counted as separate languages. A linguist called Max Weinreich made a joke famous: a language is a dialect with an army and a navy. He meant that power and history, not just grammar, decide what gets called a language.

Bhojpuri is a good example. Many people call it a dialect of [[@hindi-language|Hindi]]. But it has tens of millions of speakers and its own films and songs, and many linguists treat it as a language in its own right.

{{story:immigration-stories}}

The United States is huge, and its English varies a lot. Many southerners say "y'all" for "you all". Traditional Boston speakers often drop the "r" in words like "car". New Yorkers stand "on line" where most Americans stand "in line". The [[@soft-drinks|soft-drink]] map, pop versus soda versus coke, is a favourite of [[@usa-geography|American geography]] quizzes.

American and British English are dialects too. In 1828, Noah Webster's dictionary pushed American spellings like "color" and "center", partly to show the new country's independence. [[@english-spread|English spread]] around the world and grew new dialects, including Indian English, with its own words like "prepone" and "co-brother".

Most countries have a standard version of the language used in schools, news and government. Standard Hindi grew from Khari Boli, spoken around Delhi. Standard English grew mainly from the speech of London and southeast England.

The standard is useful because everyone can learn it. But it is not more logical than other dialects. Linguists have shown that every dialect follows consistent rules, and [[@dictionaries|dictionaries]] increasingly record regional words. Many people switch between their home dialect and the standard, depending on who they're talking to. That skill is so common, you probably do it without noticing.

text: Not quite. Emojis are a powerful way to add feeling to writing, but most linguists say they are [[@words-emoji-language|not a language on their own]]. A language needs a grammar, a shared way to combine symbols into new meanings that everyone understands. Emojis don't have one. Try telling a friend exactly what you did last Tuesday using emojis alone, and you'll soon see the problem.

Emojis work more like the gestures, faces and tone of voice we use when we talk. A laughing face after a sentence tells the reader it's a joke, the way a laugh would in person. Text messages have no tone of voice, and emojis help fill that gap.

sec.t:
The word "emoji" is Japanese: *e* means picture and *moji* means character. In 1999, a designer named Shigetaka Kurita created a set of 176 simple pictures, each just 12 [[@pixels|pixels]] square, for a Japanese mobile internet service. They included weather symbols, hearts and faces. A Japanese phone company had released an earlier set in 1997, but Kurita's became the most famous. In 2016, the Museum of [[@modern-art|Modern Art]] in New York added his 176 emojis to its collection.

Emojis went global in 2010, when they were added to Unicode, the system that lets computers everywhere show the same letters and symbols. The next year, Apple added an emoji keyboard to the iPhone, and soon emojis were on [[@smartphones|smartphones]] everywhere.

Writing has used pictures before. Egyptian [[@hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] began as pictures, but scribes soon used many of them to stand for sounds, because pictures alone couldn't say everything. [[@chinese-characters|Chinese characters]] also began partly as pictures and became a full writing system. Emojis have never made that leap, and most people don't want them to.

Emojis can be misunderstood, too. Different phones draw the same emoji differently, so a face that looks cheerful on one screen can look nervous on another. Older and younger people may read the same symbol in different ways, just as they do with [[@slang|slang]].

People do follow some patterns. Researchers who study emoji use have noticed that people often put them at the end of a sentence, like [[@words-punctuation|punctuation]], and repeat them for emphasis. A string of emojis can tell a tiny story, but only if both people already share the context.

Some linguists compare emojis with [[@sign-language|sign language]] to show what they lack. Sign languages have a full grammar, a word order and the power to make endless new sentences. Others argue that emojis are the biggest change to everyday writing in years, because they let a two-word message carry a smile. Both points can be true at once.

text: Before pens, people wrote with whatever their land gave them. In [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], scribes pressed a cut reed into wet clay. In Egypt, they painted on papyrus with reed brushes. In India and Southeast Asia, they scratched palm leaves with an iron stylus. Romans scratched wax tablets with a pointed metal or bone stick.

The tool shaped the writing. Wedges pressed in clay made cuneiform. Brushes made flowing [[@chinese-characters|Chinese characters]]. Scratches on palm leaves may have made some Indian scripts curly. Every material had its own tricks and problems.

st.prompt: Scribes in Odisha and South India scratched letters into dried palm leaves. Why might that have made their scripts round?

options.t: Long straight scratches along the leaf could split it
Round letters were faster to read aloud
Kings ordered all letters to be round

st.reveal: Palm leaves have veins running along their length. A long straight cut in that direction could tear the leaf, so curves were safer. Scripts like Odia, Telugu and Malayalam are full of rounded shapes, and many historians link this to palm-leaf writing.

sec.t:
The oldest [[@writing-began|writing]] we know of comes from Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq, around 3200 BCE. Scribes cut the end of a reed into a sharp edge and pressed it into soft clay. Each press left a wedge-shaped mark. That is why the script is called cuneiform, from the Latin word for wedge.

Clay was cheap and everywhere. A tablet could be smoothed and reused while it was wet, or dried in the sun to keep. Important ones were baked hard.

In Egypt, scribes used thin reeds chewed or cut into brushes. They dipped them in black and red [[@ink|ink]] and wrote on papyrus, made from strips of a river plant. They wrote everyday documents in fast scripts, and carved [[@hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] on temple walls.

In South and Southeast Asia, people wrote on the dried leaves of palm trees for well over a thousand years. A scribe used an iron stylus to scratch letters into the leaf. Then they rubbed soot mixed with oil over it. The black stuck in the scratches, and the rest was wiped away.

Holes were made in each leaf, and a string threaded through them to tie the pages together between wooden covers. That is why some Indian books are still called granth, from a word linked to tying.

In [[@kashmir|Kashmir]] and the Himalaya, writers used birch bark, called bhojpatra, with ink and a reed pen. Many ancient [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and Buddhist texts survive on it.

{{story:writing-began}}

Roman schoolchildren carried wax tablets: wooden boards coated with wax. They wrote with a stylus that had a point at one end and a flat end for rubbing out mistakes.

Many Indian children learned to write on a slate with chalk or a slate pencil. In parts of north India and Pakistan, children used a takhti, a wooden board coated with clay, and wrote with a reed pen called a qalam. The board could be washed and re-coated every day.

In Europe, from about the 500s CE, people wrote with quills, made from the long wing feathers of geese and swans. The tip was sharpened and split, and it wore out quickly. The word "pen" comes from the Latin word for feather.

In the 1500s, a big deposit of graphite was found at Borrowdale in England. People wrapped sticks of it in string or wood to write with. [[@pencils|Pencils]] were born. In the 1700s and 1800s, makers learned to mix powdered graphite with clay, which lets pencils be harder or softer.

In the 1800s, factories in Birmingham, England, made cheap steel nibs by the million. Fountain pens, which hold ink inside, became practical in the 1880s.

The Hungarian journalist László Bíró noticed that newspaper ink dried quickly, and worked with his brother to make a pen with a tiny rolling ball at the tip. He patented it in the 1930s. The ballpoint is now the most common pen in the world. Yet artists still love reed pens for [[@calligraphy|calligraphy]], because a cut reed makes lines no ballpoint can.
